In this VladTV interview, Rex Holloway opens up about his early life in the Houston and East Texas area before becoming a shot caller in the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas during prison—and later walking away from the gang. Holloway reflects on growing up in a two-parent home, attending gifted classes and private school, then drifting into crime as a teenager in the early 1990s. He details how shoplifting escalated into car break-ins and daytime house burglaries, often targeting guns during the crack epidemic because they could be quickly sold.  

Holloway also recounts the dangers of home invasions in Texas, including one incident where he surprised a sleeping homeowner and fled. In another burglary, he cut his arm breaking through a back door, stole firearms, and ran through the woods as the sheriff’s department tracked him with police dogs.

--------

Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza sits down with Vlad to recount a violent 1969 turning point in Los Angeles gang history. At 19, Mendoza says he went to a White Fence teen center looking for family friend David Munguia, only to be recognized, jumped, and beaten with boards and bottles. After returning to his neighborhood near the Santa Ana Freeway, he says he came back armed with a machete and killed Robert “Bobby Loco” Lopez, marking his first homicide.

Mendoza describes the emotional aftermath, a Pico Rivera house party, retaliation fears, and how a Thompson machine gun led to the temporary nickname “Machine Gun Mundo.” He also recalls being pursued by LAPD homicide detectives, hiding with Vietnam veteran Tony Sandoval, and receiving a Selective Service notice for Vietnam shortly after his arrest. A raw account of gang rivalry, regret, and life in East L.A. street culture.

Royce White sits down with Vlad to discuss his personal reaction to the killing of Charlie Kirk, saying he broke down in tears and initially questioned whether the news was real or AI-generated. White reflects on political violence in America, referencing Abraham Lincoln, Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, JFK, RFK and Ronald Reagan, while Vlad brings up his interview with John Hinckley Jr. and the Jodie Foster obsession tied to Reagan’s shooting.

The conversation also explores Kirk’s controversial comments about MLK, Black Americans and the Civil Rights Act of 1964. White says he disagreed with some of Kirk’s views, especially reliance on FBI wiretaps, but argues Kirk’s legacy as a political force remains significant. He also mentions Angela Stanton-King and questions claims surrounding Tyler Robinson, emphasizing his belief that Kirk was targeted for speaking out.
